items.content:
Notes:

- Stream 200 tokens to a user, then lose the GPU to maintenance, and you cannot just retry. Meta measures inference by cost per successful task, not per token.
- OpenAI's inference load balancer used to set its routing weights from a feedback loop. Shift traffic off a hot engine and it cools, the controller reads cool as spare capacity, and the traffic comes back. An optimizer with a view of every engine replaced it.
- The same coding agent built the same tower defense game on a closed frontier model and on an open weight model. Both games worked. FriendliAI puts the open weight run at about five and a half times cheaper.
- Superlinked's automated tuning loop produced a fine tune that cost 80 cents to train and lifted retrieval on German legal text by 18 percent, as a proof of concept.
- In Red Hat's demo a first request took about three seconds. The next turn reused the same system prompt, hit the cache on the same machine, and took about one. A new system prompt on a different machine paid the full three again.

This is the time of your life if you want to make a career in academia with minimal effort. The algorithm is simple:

1. Take any published paper.

2. Go to the "Future Work" section.

3. Task an agent with designing an experiment based on the future work text and run it.

4. Once the experiment provides results that are at least marginally better than those shown in the other paper, task an agent with writing a follow-up paper.

5. Submit to all second- and third-tier conferences.

6. Repeat the process thousands of times per month.

The law of large numbers always works.

items.content:
I believe nation states will keep becoming less and less relevant and that in the future everyone will be a nomad

Most nation states (and well governments) barely function anymore through 100+ years of democratic baggage from laws and regulation that can't be reversed

People can't save their countries or governments anymore through people's initiatives or getting into politics, because the systems are so old and in full gridlock

Globalism has deservedly gotten a really bad rep the last 5 years though as we were too naive about it, but I think we should keep the good parts from it

We should not take our identity from or defer our individual power to nation states ran by a political mafia class that's just perpetual robbing us and has no intention (or ability!) to actually improve society

Nation states are a relatively new invention and barely 150 years old, before we had empires, kingdoms, smaller city states (kinda like municipalities) and tribes or local communities

Over the years I've been increasingly red-pilled by @oskarth that nation states simply do not work and you need smaller sizes of government for things to work efficiently. Once it gets too big you get too much regulation and Kafka-esque bureaucracy and you end up with gridlock

Which is Europe's entire problem right now!

There's some exceptions, US and China seem to operate at large scale and are doing relatively well considering their size

Anyway to get back to my point, I think it's preferable people think of themselves as global citizens, because it gives them stronger negotiation power in relation to nation states and governments as they're able to pack up and leave to where they're treated better

And having people be mobile then also incentivizes other nation states (or smaller types of governance) to compete with them to attract the best people, and in response the other states will improve to attract people back

Now with geopolitical tensions (like the stuff about Russia and Europe this week), it shows even more the benefit to be able to pack your bag and leave to a better place quickly is an extreme benefit now and in the future, possibly even for survival

items.content:
Blockchain is to crypto what the internet is to email. One made the other famous, but the technology can do much more.

Crypto is one application; blockchain can also help organizations share records and verify information across companies without one owner.

Microblog @antgrasso

Forget crypto for a moment.

Imagine three companies working on the same supply chain. Each keeps its own records, so they spend time checking which version is correct.

With blockchain, they can share a record of what happened. Each update follows agreed rules, and previous entries are difficult to change without the others noticing.

A product can carry a shared history as it moves between companies.

A digital credential can be issued by one organization and verified by another.

A smart contract can trigger an action when a defined condition is met.

Crypto uses the same technology to record and transfer digital value. It is one application, not the definition of blockchain.

The question is: do several parties need to share and verify the same record without giving one of them control?

If yes, blockchain may be worth considering.

#Blockchain #DigitalTrust

items.content:
Grigori Perelman - Instagram - The only Millennium Prize Problem ever solved so far was solved by a human mathematician who refused both the Mathematical Fields Medal and the $1 million prize

In 2002–2003, Perelman quietly posted a series of papers on arXiv, presenting a solution in just 70 pages.

Before asking whether AGI could solve the remaining Millennium Prize Problems, it is worth remembering the there is a human mathematician who already solved millennium prize problem. 

Grigori Perelman solved the Henri Poincaré-Conjecture, a problem posed by Henri Poincaré in 1900 and later selected as the 7 Clay Millennium Prize Problems. 

Perelman published his breakthrough work in 2002–2003, building on Richard Hamilton’s Ricci-flow program. After years of verification by mathematicians, the mathematical community accepted the proof.

In 2006, Perelman declined the Fields Medal. The prize money was approximately $10,000. 

In 2010, the Clay Mathematics Institute awarded him the $1 million Millennium Prize for solving the Poincaré Conjecture. 

He declined that both prizes. Clay’s own historical record confirms both refusals.

That makes Perelman an extraordinary benchmark for the AGI era.

The only human mathematician, working with deep geometric intuition and ideas developed across generations, solved a problem that resisted mathematics for almost a century.

So the only Millennium Prize Problem solved so far was solved by a human mathematician who ultimately placed the mathematics itself above medals, and the monetary prize attached to it. He said his math purity and integrity goes above and beyond $1M prize and Fields Medal.  He said the solution itself is considered as reward.
